raw_summary:
You can now stream generative UI from your Chat SDK agent with json-render.

With a typed catalog of components, the agent writes a JSON spec that json-render converts into a Chat SDK card. Each adapter then posts the card in its platform’s native format, such as Block Kit on Slack and Adaptive Cards on Teams.

The catalog covers tables, charts, buttons, and more, so there’s no separate tool to build and maintain for each message shape.

Stream cards as the model writes

streamCard posts the card once its root element has content and updates the message as new elements stream in. Edits go out at most once every 500 ms by default, which matches Chat SDK’s streaming interval. Once the stream ends, the message shows the final, validated card.

Validate specs and enforce platform limits

toCard checks every element’s props against its component schema and throws CardSpecError for an invalid spec. Each problem gets its own readable issue, so you can send the list back to the model for a corrected spec.

Platforms cap what a single message can hold, and Chat SDK adapters degrade content past those caps. The Slack adapter, for example, turns a second table into a code block. Pass limits to reject those specs instead.

Read the documentation to get started, or try the playground.

Read more
title: Chat SDK agents can now stream generative UI with json-render

raw_summary:
What's changed

  • Changed auto mode with telemetry or feature flags off, including behind LLM gateways: calls the server can't check are asked about or denied, with no fallback to the built-in classifier; set CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_MODE_SERVER=0 to keep using it (Bedrock, Vertex and Foundry are unchanged)
  • Changed auto mode behind an LLM gateway: CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_MODE_SERVER=1 turns on the server-side check even with CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_EXPERIMENTAL_BETAS set; if managed settings set the latter, they must set the 1 too
  • Added support for MCP tasks in the terminal: when an MCP server runs a tool call as a task, Claude Code moves it to the background right away and tells Claude the result when it finishes
  • Added the CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_MCP_TASK_BACKGROUND environment variable to make Claude Code wait for an MCP task inside its tool call instead of moving it to the background right away
  • Added permissions.denyInsteadOfPrompting setting: a tool call that would wait on a permission prompt is denied and the turn continues, in terminal sessions, subagents and teammates
  • Added /claude-api latency-optimize to find where your Claude API code makes people wait and try faster settings against your eval
  • Added the CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_FEATURE_FLAGS environment variable, which stops feature-flag fetching without turning off telemetry; every flag then uses its built-in default
  • Added spend for today, this week and this month to /usage for developers behind a Claude apps gateway who have no spend limit, when the gateway runs this version or later
  • Added admin.pooled_conflict_rule and admin.pooled_priority_order to the Claude apps gateway, to set which pooled group budget pays first for a developer in several groups
  • Added an optional login_notice setting to the Claude apps gateway that shows an operator-defined message on the gateway's browser verification page and on Claude Code's sign-in screen
  • Added CLAUDE_GATEWAY_LOG_FORMAT=json to the Claude apps gateway: operational log lines become JSON with severity, time and message, for log collectors that read the level from a field
  • Added a Claude apps gateway boot warning for a case where another policy's availableModels also allows a custom model id that one policy lists by name
  • Added start-up warnings to the Claude apps gateway for policies with no desktopHome that rely on coworkTabEnabled: false or chatSessionRetentionDays, ahead of Claude Desktop's November 10 change
  • Added a warning when your claude.ai login ends and Claude Code continues on the sign-in from ant auth login, which bills usage to your Claude Console organization
  • Added a line at startup naming the Claude Console organization that is billed in a case where Claude Code uses the sign-in from ant auth login

raw_summary:
Ampersand from Humans& is now available on AI Gateway for free through November 13, 2026.

Ampersand is a language model built to take part in group conversations, such as a team chat, and to decide on each turn whether to speak or stay quiet. It is designed to understand individual and shared goals, help people work through disagreements, and recognize when a contribution would be useful. That can mean asking a clarifying question, sharing relevant context, or waiting while people respond to one another.

Your application exposes these actions as caller-defined function tools. send_message delivers a contribution, while pass leaves the conversation quiet until the next human message. Your application executes both tools and records their results. Leave tool choice at its default, since Ampersand accepts auto and none but rejects required and named tool choices.

Call it through the AI SDK, the OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API, or a coding agent. Use humansand/ampersand-v0.1 as the model name:

The first human message invites a contribution; the second asks Ampersand to wait. In a chat application, call the handler when a new human message arrives. Handling pass records the waiting action without posting a message or starting another model turn. For a deployed chat application, persist the response, history, and delivery receipts in durable storage. Retry uncertain delivery with the saved action and the same receipt, process messages sequentially per conversation, and check conversation access before posting.

To use it in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and more, install the latest Vercel CLI and run setup:

Then select humansand/ampersand-v0.1 in the agent. See the coding agents guide for details.

Try Ampersand in the model playground.

AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries, failover, and performance optimizations for higher-than-provider uptime. It includes built-in custom reporting, budgets for API keys, routing rules, and more.

AI Gateway reflects provider pricing with no markup and does not charge a platform fee on inference, including on Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) requests.

You can view all language models available on AI Gateway.

Read more

raw_summary:
Data Cloud connectors in Gemini for business, now in preview, give business users and analysts a direct way to query live enterprise data in natural language. Across most organizations, data questions multiply faster than analysts can answer them: Projects stall in ticket queues, leaders fall back on guesswork, and unmanaged spreadsheets spread across teams. Early generative AI tools promised conversational access to data, but they often struggled to generate accurate SQL across complex schemas or to respect governance rules. Data Cloud connectors let you query governed data directly from your workspace while enforcing row- and column-level security and respecting end-user credentials.

A new way to query enterprise data

Gemini brings conversational analytics directly into your day-to-day workflow through two paths: Conversational Analytics agents, which let you create data agents that include context and instructions to effectively answer questions for specific use cases, and Data Cloud connectors, allowing you to query live data directly with Gemini. End users can pull data directly from BigQuery (preview), operational databases like Spanner, AlloyDB, and Cloud SQL (preview), and governed data from Looker (preview). From there, you can move your findings directly into everyday tools, such as turning query results into a Google Doc, an email draft in Gmail, or a deck in Google Slides.

How Data Cloud connectors work

Data Cloud connectors work with Knowledge Catalog to locate relevant data, interpret your question, and execute permission-scoped queries under your identity.

When you ask a question in Gemini, the system coordinates discovery, semantic interpretation, and query execution, using the following capabilities:

  1. Natural-language question: You ask an exploratory question in plain language (for example, "How many sales did we have this month for all cold weather products?"). End users aren’t expected to know the table or project to use.

  2. Semantic discovery: Gemini searches Knowledge Catalog to locate candidate data across your estate, considering key attributes like usage patterns.

  3. Context mapping: The system uses technical metadata, business glossaries, and semantic models to map everyday terms into exact database structures, such as resolving "cold weather products" to specific categories like sweaters, coats, and jackets in an ecommerce catalog.

  4. Permission-aware execution: Gemini generates a SQL query and runs it through the connector under your user credentials, respecting your existing row- and column-level database permissions.

To accurately navigate an enterprise data estate, language models need business context alongside raw database access. Knowledge Catalog provides a curated context bundle, including technical metadata, business logic, table relationships, and verified queries, that improves query accuracy while reducing latency and token consumption.

Enterprise analytics has long been fragmented by physical borders: data locked in proprietary silos, open lakehouse tables in cloud object storage, and datasets distributed across multicloud environments. Beyond native BigQuery storage, the BigQuery connector brings conversational analytics to a borderless lakehouse, unifying these environments into a single conversational interface to query open table formats (including Apache Iceberg, Delta Lake, and Parquet) and cross-cloud datasets in AWS or Azure using BigQuery. The connector inherits fine-grained access policies from BigQuery and Knowledge Catalog, so row- and column-level access controls apply whether you query native tables or open lakehouse files.

Choosing between connectors and data agents

In addition to using direct Data Cloud connectors to query data in plain language, you can also use Conversational Analytics agents to enable these experiences. While Data Cloud connectors allow you to provide exploratory and ad hoc analysis for users, conversational analytics agents are scoped agents that are built and certified directly by data teams within your organization. These can be built across Data Cloud products such as BigQuery, Looker, and operational databases including Spanner, AlloyDB, and Cloud SQL.

These pre-configured agents allow users to run highly governed, multi-step strategic analyses that are scoped to particular subsets of data, supporting compliance requirements and predictable results for reporting. These data agents can also be published in Gemini for consumption or made available via API for building your own conversational apps in the enterprise.

These approaches are complementary. Gemini direct connectivity also surfaces relevant published agents created by central data teams, so users can decide whether to proceed with ad hoc analysis using the connectors or use the scoped agent. You can choose the right approach for each workload.

Built-in access controls and governance

Data Cloud connector queries execute under the end user’s identity. An employee without access to executive salary data or protected healthcare records cannot query that data through natural-language prompts. The agent only discovers metadata in Knowledge Catalog to which you have access, and only executes queries that your account has permission to run.

How to create Data Cloud connectors

Administrators can configure Data Cloud connectors in the Gemini admin console. From there, admins set up default read-only connections to datasets in BigQuery, operational databases, or Looker, with Knowledge Catalog enabled automatically. Once configured, end users can enable the connector in Gemini to start querying data and building reports in plain language.

Setup documentation is available for the BigQuery, Spanner, Cloud SQL, and AlloyDB for PostgreSQL connectors, with Looker also in preview.

Unlike data ingestion mode, which copies data into a Gemini data store, Data Cloud connectors use federated query mode to query your data in place without copying or indexing it — using Knowledge Catalog automatically to search accessible metadata and look up business context.

Why use Data Cloud connectors over custom MCP

Compared to connecting to public or self-managed Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, first-party Data Cloud connectors provide two main advantages:

  1. Built-in skills for higher response quality: Data Cloud connectors include pre-configured agent skills tailored to each data engine, such as advanced SQL and AI function generation for BigQuery and operational databases, to improve query accuracy and response quality.

  2. Guided setup and managed authentication: First-party connectors provide a guided setup experience with managed authentication for Google Cloud databases and BigQuery, removing the need to deploy MCP middleware or manage your own OAuth client configuration for Google Cloud services. In addition, connector-specific settings, such as specifying a default Google Cloud billing project for BigQuery query execution, help administrators enforce governance and manage query costs.

Get started today

Data Cloud connectors help teams find answers from enterprise data sources without waiting on backlog queues. To get started, review the Data Cloud connectors documentation or explore Conversational Analytics agents.
source: Google Cloud AI and Machine Learning Blog
title: Bringing conversational analytics to Gemini with Agentic Data Cloud connectors

DeepSeek Search and DeepSeek Fetch are now available through AI Gateway. Search finds relevant pages with titles, URLs, and summaries. Fetch retrieves page content as Markdown for your model to read.

Use both tools with any model that supports tool calling, using one AI Gateway API key. No separate DeepSeek account is required, and you can keep the same tools when switching model providers.

These helpers are available in AI SDK 6.0.321 and later on v6, or 7.0.160 and later on v7. Update with pnpm add ai@latest and set your AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY. To combine search and page retrieval, pass both helpers in tools:

You can also use alternative search tools with DeepSeek Fetch if DeepSeek Search fails:

Search fallback is model-directed, so provider order and retry limits are best effort. DeepSeek Fetch can retrieve a result URL from any of these search tools.

Search and Fetch each cost $0.75 per 1,000 billable requests. Failed requests, timeouts, and empty results have no tool charge. Model tokens are billed separately.

See the DeepSeek Search documentation and DeepSeek Fetch documentation for configuration options and pricing details.

AI Gateway provides one API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring routing, retries, and failover. You can use an AI Gateway API key or bring your own provider key.

raw_summary:
Vercel Tracing is now generally available on all plans. You can now search and inspect traces from the dashboard or the Vercel CLI, and new Next.js projects get tracing by default. Pricing is unchanged from the beta.

Browse and search traces in the dashboard

In beta, you could only open a trace per request from the Logs page. The new Traces page shows every trace and span in one place, for a project or your whole team. Switch between a Spans list and a Traces list, filter each, and search with Kibana Query Language (KQL). A Live mode streams new traces as they arrive. A query like span.name:db* AND span.duration > 500 narrows to slow database spans by name and duration.

Search traces from the CLI

The Traces page uses the same KQL as vercel traces search --query, so a query built in the dashboard runs in the CLI unchanged. Search covers every project in your team, or one project with the --project flag. Inspect a single trace with vercel traces inspect <request-id>, and manage a project's sampling rules with vercel traces config.

Automatic tracing for new Next.js projects

In beta, nothing was collected until you added a sampling rule. Starting with Next.js 16.5, new projects created on Vercel that include at least one Node.js function get tracing turned on after their first successful build. Vercel adds one sampling rule tracing 100% of requests in all environments and injects instrumentation at build time, so traces include Next.js framework spans with no setup. To opt out, remove all sampling rules in Settings → Tracing.

Longer retention

In beta, traces followed your runtime log retention. Hobby now keeps traces for 3 days instead of 1 hour, Pro for 14 days instead of 1 day, and Enterprise for 14 days instead of 3 days.

Read the Tracing documentation to learn more.

Read more
title: Vercel Tracing is now generally available

raw_summary:
Welcome back to The Blueprint, a regular feature where we highlight how Google Cloud customers are tackling unique and common challenges across industries using the latest AI and cloud technologies. We hope to inspire others looking to innovate in their work.

AI is rapidly transforming video production at virtually every step of the process, from ideation and storyboarding to filming, editing, and release. At Mito, we’re striving to democratize AI-powered video creation, enabling everyone from solo artists to large enterprises to get the most out of the best creative technologies available.

The Challenge

When we founded Mito, our goal was to eliminate the complex technical friction that stops creators from telling long-form, narrative stories with generative AI. 

However, transitioning from a single five-second clip to a cohesive campaign — such as a 120-second national TV spot for Movistar Plus+, a part of Telefónica, to broadcast across Spain during the World Cup this summer. This effort revealed massive infrastructure and workflow bottlenecks:

  • Asset & workflow overhead: Managing local media libraries across individual workstations was unscalable. For Movistar alone, our production required generating a massive "iceberg" of over 5000 assets (1000 of those videos) generated in around 65 iteration rounds.

  • Zero real-time collaboration: Traditional feedback loops required manual downloads, Google Drive uploads, and fragmented communication across chat apps and email.

  • Rendering latency: Standard AI video rendering takes four to five minutes per short clip. Running these processes synchronously froze our user interface and stalled creative velocity.

  • Model disparity & consistency: Every generative model requires distinct prompting logic. Maintaining character persistence, specific lighting, and camera angles across dozens of shots — while preserving the likeness of real public figures like chef Ferran Adrià or journalist Juanma Castaño — was nearly impossible without central orchestration.

  • Capacity constraints: Operating on public pay-as-you-go model APIs left us vulnerable to rate limits and regional throughput throttling during peak traffic.

The Solution

To deliver an infinite, real-time creative canvas for filmmakers, we designed a serverless, asynchronous architecture built on Google Cloud.

We run our API, AI Director, and background workers as Java services on Cloud Run, which scales with request volume.

In order to address message routing challenges, we decoupled job execution using Google Cloud Pub/Sub as our central event bus. Long-running video generations are offloaded to background Cloud Run workers, allowing creators to keep working uninterrupted on the UI canvas.

To minimize latency, media assets are stored in Google Cloud Storage and delivered via Cloud CDN. Expiring key signatures keep pre-release client assets strictly private. Keeping our storage alongside the models we call through Vertex AI reduces network transfer delays.

An isolated database architecture helps with the heavy business intelligence and analytics workloads while mitigating potential negative impacts on production performance through Cloud SQL and PostgreSQL. We rely heavily on foundational models like Omni, Veo and Nano Banana, which we access through Vertex AI alongside our custom system prompts.

Finally, our structured canvas frontend enforces a "Rule of 6" (limiting prompt variables across World, Camera, Light, Texture, Actions, and Character) and prioritizes still-frame generation before video rendering to maximize cost efficiency.

The Architecture

The Outcome

By pairing our creative orchestration platform with Google Cloud’s infrastructure, we successfully delivered a landmark national broadcast campaign that the production team describes as 95% AI-generated:

  • Prime-time scale: The 120-second Movistar campaign for the Spanish National Team  aired across every major television channel in Spain, with 1,441 assets live on a single shared Canvas near launch.

  • AI Director copilot: Our conversational agent translates natural language instructions into precise model parameters while maintaining context, lighting, and visual style across every scene.

  • Seamless collaboration: Distributed teams and brand clients can work on the same canvas in real time. Because new generations are saved as separate assets instead of overwriting earlier ones, stakeholders can duplicate projects to explore parallel creative ideas.

  • Continuous dogfooding: Through our internal studio, Mito Films, we put our tools to the test on high-stakes client projects — whether that's global television spots or keynotes for top robotics startups — ensuring direct feedback flows back into engineering.

  • Future-proof foundation: Our architecture is primed for rendering times to collapse from minutes to seconds, positioning Mito to handle upcoming world models, deeper memory states, and personalized content delivery.

The Details

Building an enterprise-grade platform for AI storytelling required solving several backend and creative challenges. This includes our creation of a virtual queuing system that mitigates third-party API rate limiting during usage spikes for smooth request concurrency, with bounded retries and a clear outcome for every job.

Because creative output cannot be fully validated with standard unit tests, we built an automated evaluation harness powered by Gemini. Acting as an independent judge, it evaluates AI Director outputs against original user intents across an automated test suite, which we run alongside standard tests for high-impact Director changes.

We knew early on that we would need multi-model intelligence routing. As such, we built the AI Director to dynamically coordinate tasks across multiple specialized models — including Sonnet, Gemini, and ElevenLabs for audio — treating the spatial canvas like a live code repository to infer adjacent contextual cues.

We also needed to embrace an “imperfect aesthetic” to arrive at a more authentic outcome. In our Movistar spot, the story follows Tommy, a 17-year-old student making an AI video project. At the climax, the AI misunderstands a prompt, making coach Luis de la Fuente say "In the same milkshake" while holding a drink. Tommy edits the prompt live to "In the same heartbeat," and the video recalibrates instantly. 

By incorporating surreal visual elements — like stadium stands built into Galician cliffs or a neighborhood bar covered in pitch grass — we showcased how generative AI can elevate human storytelling rather than obscure it.
source: Google Cloud AI and Machine Learning Blog
title: The Blueprint: Orchestrating 5,000+ AI assets for a World Cup TV spot

The products aren't good enough to sell people on the costs.

You cannot tell people that you have to listen to the whine of a data center in their backyard for AI overviews and some of the most hilarious deep fake slop in history.

It's not worth it. It just isn't worth it to anyone. And agents aren't real and they might not be being used the way that anyone wants them to yet. All these companies are spending more than they're making on these products. Refrigerators holding blood storage in Europe are being hacked.

The costs are too high. The benefits are not real. And if you connect that to corruption, you're like, in order to impose these costs on me, these CEOs are in the White House shaking Trump's hand, renaming it to the Gulf of America, paying for this ballroom that we don't want. It's obvious crypto-corruption, and it's still slop.

The AI industry will not get out of it until they make better products. Until everyone can see without needing to be convinced, without needing an ad campaign, without any of this stuff that just using these products makes your life better.

— Nilay Patel, The Vergecast: Big Tech lost big in the 2026 election

raw_summary:
You can now set a new project to expire when you deploy it with Vercel CLI. Expired projects are deleted automatically, so prototypes, demos, and test apps don't need cleaning up by hand.

Run vercel deploy with --delete-project-after and a duration:

Supported durations are 1h, 1d, 1w, 2w, and 30d, and the CLI prints the date and time when the project expires. The flag only applies when vercel deploy creates the project. If you deploy to an existing project with the flag, its expiration doesn't change and the CLI prints a warning.

To remove a project's expiration, run vercel project keep:

Update Vercel CLI to v65.12.0 or later to get started. Learn more in the vercel deploy documentation.

title: Vercel CLI can now set new projects to expire
